title: itertools: Combinatorics & Chaining
blurb: Flatten, enumerate, and group: iterator tools that replace index arithmetic with pipelines that state what they mean.

cells.title: chain: many sequences, one pass
cells.body:
Real data rarely arrives as one flat list: logs come in hourly files, batches in chunks, edges in per-node buckets. Before you can scan anything you must flatten — and the classic mistake is to flatten by copying: nested loops that append into a fresh list, index bookkeeping, off-by-one bugs at batch boundaries.

chain.from_iterable(batches) yields every element of every batch in order, lazily, with no copying and no indices — and unlike chain(*batches) it does not need all batches up front, so it works on generators too. Flattening is the simplest example of a broader idea: composing iterators into a pipeline where each stage pulls from the previous one. The moment you stop managing indices, whole categories of bugs disappear.

demo.code:
from itertools import chain

batches = [[1, 2], [], [3], [4, 5]]
print(list(chain.from_iterable(batches)))

def in_batches(items, size):
    for i in range(0, len(items), size):
        yield items[i:i + size]

print(list(chain.from_iterable(in_batches(range(1, 8), 3))))

cells.title: Combinatorial iterators: enumerate the universe, then filter
cells.body:
Some questions sound like clever puzzles — which menu combinations hit the budget exactly, what numbers can these digits form, which subsets satisfy the rule — but when the universe of candidates is small, the honest answer is to enumerate every candidate and test it. The combinatorial iterators are candidate factories: product walks every way to pick one item per list, permutations every arrangement, combinations every subset of a given size.

The skill being trained is not memorizing the functions; it is estimating the size of the universe before committing. Six options per course across five courses is under eight thousand meals — enumerable. Twenty items choose ten is 184,756 — still fine. A 40-character alphabet permuted is not. Enumeration converts a reasoning problem into a counting problem, and counting is where you catch trouble early.

demo.code:
from itertools import product, permutations, combinations

print(list(product([1, 2], ["a", "b"])))
print(list(permutations("ab")))
print(list(combinations([1, 2, 3], 2)))
print("meals:", len(list(product(range(6), repeat=5))))

cells.title: groupby groups consecutive runs — sort first
cells.body:
groupby walks a sequence and yields a (key, group) pair for every run of consecutive elements that share the same key. That is the contract, and it is the most misunderstood line in the module: it does not find all elements matching a key — only the adjacent ones. Feed it unsorted words and one letter's words arrive scattered across several tiny groups.

The fix is the pattern to memorize: sort by the same key you group by, then group. Python's sort is stable, so elements that share a key keep their original relative order inside the sorted run — sorting does not scramble your data, it concentrates it. The same discipline applies whenever you reach for grouping: decide the key, order by the key, then group.

demo.code:
from itertools import groupby

words = ["pear", "fig", "plum", "apple", "peach"]
key = lambda w: w[0]

naive = [(k, list(g)) for k, g in groupby(words, key)]
print(naive)

ordered = sorted(words, key=key)
fixed = [(k, list(g)) for k, g in groupby(ordered, key)]
print(fixed)

exercise.title: One conveyor, many batches
exercise.statement:
A sorting facility logs parcels hour by hour: the day's data is a list of batches, one list per hour, each holding that hour's parcel ids in scan order. Some hours are idle and contribute an empty batch.

Rebuild the full day as a single flat list of parcel ids, preserving the original order exactly — hour by hour, and within each hour, scan by scan.
constraints: every batch holds between 0 and 1,000 ids

examples.why: empty hours contribute nothing; everything else keeps its place
batches are concatenated in the order they appear

tests.label: mixed batches with an empty one

hints: A nested loop with append works — but the module has a tool whose whole job is 'yield everything from everything, in order'. What is it?
itertools.chain.from_iterable(batches) takes an iterable of iterables and yields their elements one batch at a time, without copying or index math.
return list(chain.from_iterable(batches)) materializes the flattened stream. It also works when batches is a generator, unlike chain(*batches).
exercise.reasoning: Flattening is concatenation in disguise: the result is 'batch 0's items, then batch 1's, then batch 2's'. A nested loop expresses that, but it also makes you own the bookkeeping — the loop variables, the append calls, the temptation to name an index. chain.from_iterable states the intent (stream everything, in order) and is lazy: it pulls one batch at a time, so memory stays flat no matter how many batches arrive. The transferable instinct is to see 'many containers, one sequence' as a pipeline stage rather than a loop shape — the same thinking later turns into generator pipelines that process log files without ever holding a full day in memory.

exercise.title: Hit the lunch budget exactly
exercise.statement:
A cafeteria build-your-own-meal station sells meals in courses: the menu is a list of courses, and each course offers a list of (item_name, price) options. A meal is formed by picking exactly one option from every course.

The accounting team can only reimburse meals that cost exactly the daily budget — one cent over or under is rejected. Return every budget-exact meal as a list of item-name tuples, listed in menu-sweep order: like an odometer, the last course's options cycle fastest.
constraints: each course offers between 1 and 6 options
prices are integers between 1 and 50; 1 <= budget <= 300

examples.why: soup+pasta is 4+9 and salad+wrap is 6+7; the other two combinations miss 13
the only possible meal costs 2, so nothing hits the budget

exercise.starter:
def exact_meals(courses, budget):
    """Return all meals whose prices sum exactly to budget.

    A meal picks one option per course; meals appear
    in menu-sweep order (last course cycles fastest).
    """
    pass

tests.label: two exact meals out of four

hints: How would you list every possible meal by hand for three courses — and is the count small enough to simply check each one?
Enumerate all candidate meals with itertools.product, one option per course, then keep exactly those whose prices sum to the budget.
for combo in product(*courses): total = sum(price for _, price in combo); keep tuple(name for name, _ in combo) when total == budget. The tuples come out in menu-sweep order automatically.
exercise.reasoning: The problem defines the answer set implicitly ('one option per course, total equals budget'), and enumeration makes that definition executable: product(*courses) is literally 'one option per course, all ways'. Correctness then rests on one countable fact — the number of meals is the product of the option counts, at most 6 to the power 6 here — so brute force is not a gamble, it is a budgeted decision. The alternative (index arithmetic per course, nested loops that change shape with the course count) is exactly the code that breaks when a seventh course appears. Learning to size the universe first is what separates deliberate enumeration from accidental exponential blowup.
exercise.solution:
from itertools import product


def exact_meals(courses, budget):
    """Return all meals whose prices sum exactly to budget.

    A meal picks one option per course; meals appear
    in menu-sweep order (last course cycles fastest).
    """
    meals = []
    for combo in product(*courses):
        if sum(price for _, price in combo) == budget:
            meals.append(tuple(name for name, _ in combo))
    return meals

exercise.title: Autocomplete index
exercise.statement:
A search box suggests words as you type. To power it, build an index that groups words by their first letter: return a list of (letter, words) pairs where the letters are in alphabetical order and each group lists its words in their original order of appearance.

The word list arrives as an OpCountList — a list stand-in that counts how many times your code inspects an element. Your algorithm may inspect elements at most 3 x len(words) times, so a plan that re-scans the whole list once per letter of the alphabet will blow the budget on the big hidden test.
constraints: words are non-empty lowercase strings; duplicates are allowed
inspection budget: at most 3 x len(words) element inspections (len() itself is free)

examples.why: letters sort alphabetically; inside 'p', the original order pear, plum, peach is preserved
output letters are sorted, not in first-seen order

exercise.starter:
def first_letter_index(words):
    """Group words by first letter for the search index.

    Letters appear alphabetically; words inside a group
    keep their original order. words is an OpCountList:
    inspecting an element costs 1, so touch each element
    as few times as possible.
    """
    pass

tests.label: all words share one letter, with duplicates

hints: Grouping tools that walk a sequence only cluster CONSECUTIVE equals. What must be true of the input's order before they can group a letter's words together?
Sort by the same key you group by — Python's sort is stable, so words sharing a first letter keep their original relative order inside the sorted run.
ordered = sorted(words, key=lambda w: w[0]) is one pass; then groupby(ordered, key=lambda w: w[0]) yields (letter, group) pairs — materialize each group with list(group).
exercise.reasoning: The trap is that grouping tools only see adjacent equal keys, so the real work happens before the grouping: sorting by the same key concentrates each letter's words into one contiguous run. The stability of Python's sort is what preserves 'original order of appearance' inside each run — a stable sort never reorders equal keys, so the sorted sequence keeps the story the input told. The budget enforces the discipline: re-scanning the list once per letter costs 26 inspections per word, while sort-then-group touches each word once. 'Sort by the grouping key' is the contract to remember — forget it and the code still runs, it just quietly returns dozens of fragment groups instead of one per key.
exercise.solution:
from itertools import groupby


def first_letter_index(words):
    """Group words by first letter for the search index.

    Letters appear alphabetically; words inside a group
    keep their original order. words is an OpCountList:
    inspecting an element costs 1, so touch each element
    as few times as possible.
    """
    ordered = sorted(words, key=lambda w: w[0])
    return [(letter, list(group))
            for letter, group in groupby(ordered, key=lambda w: w[0])]

exercise.title: Combination lock: next code
exercise.statement:
A bike lock shows a number built from digit stickers — no zeros, up to seven stickers. You may peel off every sticker and restick them in any arrangement; every sticker must be used exactly once.

Find the smallest number strictly greater than the one currently shown that can be displayed this way, and return it as an integer. If every rearrangement is smaller than or equal to the current number, return -1.
constraints: digits contains only the characters 1-9 (no zeros)
duplicates among the stickers are allowed

examples.why: the arrangements are 125, 152, 215, 251, 512, 521; the smallest one above 215 is 251
778, 787 and 877 are the only distinct arrangements; 787 is the smallest one above 778

hints: How many distinct arrangements can seven stickers have at most? Could you afford to look at every single one of them?
itertools.permutations(digits) yields every arrangement as a tuple of characters. Join each into a string, convert to int, and keep the smallest value that is strictly greater than the shown number.
Track best = None while looping; update it when value is above int(digits) and smaller than the current best. Return best if found, otherwise -1. At most 5040 arrangements for seven stickers.
exercise.reasoning: This is a search problem in disguise, and the key move is sizing the universe before choosing a strategy: seven stickers admit at most 7! = 5040 arrangements, so scanning them all is instant and — more importantly — obviously correct. A single loop with a running minimum states the whole argument; there is no index surgery to get wrong. The clever linear-time rearrangement trick exists, but it is easy to misapply on duplicates and it wins nothing at this input size. The transferable judgment: enumeration is not a dirty word — it is a deliberate trade that buys correctness with a countable, bounded amount of work. The failure mode to avoid is running the same sweep on twenty stickers, where the universe is 2.4 quintillion and the plan silently stops being a plan.
